claims.claim: Wisdom found in non-Christian thinkers, philosophy and literature can lead toward the truth, and Christians should study it.

stances.summary: Every true thing any thinker ever said came from the Word, the same Word who became man in Christ. So whatever the philosophers and poets said well already belongs to Christians.
stances.quote: For each man spoke well in proportion to the share he had of the spermatic word, seeing what was related to it. But they who contradict themselves on the more important points appear not to have possessed the heavenly wisdom, and the knowledge which cannot be spoken against. Whatever things were rightly said among all men, are the property of us Christians.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods and George Reith, ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written at Rome c. 150-160 by a convert who kept wearing the philosopher's cloak. The same passage qualifies the praise: the teachings of Plato are 'not in all respects similar' to Christ's, and the writers saw 'darkly'. In First Apology 46 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0126.htm) he says 'those who lived reasonably are Christians, even though they have been thought atheists; as, among the Greeks, Socrates and Heraclitus'. In Dialogue with Trypho 2 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/01281.htm) he calls philosophy 'the greatest possession, and most honourable before God', and in chapter 8 says of Christianity 'I found this philosophy alone to be safe and profitable'. Martyred c. 165. His pupil Tatian took the opposite line.

stances.summary: God gave philosophy to the Greeks the way He gave the Law to the Jews, as a tutor to lead them to Christ. Now it still helps faith, as training for the mind.
stances.quote: Accordingly, before the advent of the Lord, philosophy was necessary to the Greeks for righteousness. And now it becomes conducive to piety; being a kind of preparatory training to those who attain to faith through demonstration.
stances.translation: William Wilson, ANF vol. 2, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Alexandria, c. 198-203. The same chapter goes on: 'For this was a schoolmaster to bring the Hellenic mind, as the law, the Hebrews, to Christ.' In 1.20 philosophy does not make truth stronger but is 'the proper fence and wall of the vineyard' against sophistry. His qualification: philosophy is 'preparatory', faith is the bread. Strom. 1 also reports the other camp in his own day: 'The Hellenic philosophy then, according to some, apprehended the truth accidentally, dimly, partially; as others will have it, was set a-going by the devil.' Clement was never condemned, but his name was dropped from the Roman Martyrology in the 16th century.

stances.summary: Take from Greek philosophy whatever can prepare the mind for Christianity, the way Israel took gold from Egypt to build God's tabernacle. Philosophy should serve the faith as a handmaid.
stances.quote: The children of the philosophers speak of geometry and music and grammar and rhetoric and astronomy as being ancillary to philosophy; and in the same way we might speak of philosophy itself as being ancillary to Christianity.
stances.translation: Allan Menzies, ANF vol. 9, 1896 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: Letter to Gregory (preserved in the Philocalia, chapter 13)
stances.location: section 1 (the Egyptian spoils follow in section 2)
stances.context: Written c. 235 to his former pupil Gregory (later Thaumaturgus). The previous sentence: 'I would wish that you should take with you on the one hand those parts of the philosophy of the Greeks which are fit, as it were, to serve as general or preparatory studies for Christianity'. Section 2 is the origin of the 'spoiling the Egyptians' reading, with a warning: 'there are few who have taken of the useful things of Egypt and come out of it', and the story of 'Ader' (Hadad) the Edomite who went down to Egypt and came back to make idols. Section 3: 'study first of all the divine Scriptures'. Heterodox status: several of Origen's speculative teachings (pre-existence of souls, universal restoration) were condemned after his death, above all in 553. His own practice is described by Gregory Thaumaturgus (see that entry).

stances.summary: A student should read everything the philosophers and poets wrote, rejecting nothing except the atheists, so that no single school captures the mind. Gregory says his teacher Origen was wise to train him this way.
stances.quote: For he deemed it right for us to study philosophy in such wise, that we should read with utmost diligence all that has been written, both by the philosophers and by the poets of old, rejecting nothing, and repudiating nothing (for, indeed, we did not yet possess the power of critical discernment), except only the productions of the atheists
stances.translation: S. D. F. Salmond, ANF vol. 6, 1886 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: Oration and Panegyric Addressed to Origen
stances.context: Delivered c. 238-239 when Gregory left Origen's school at Caesarea. It is a pupil's first-hand record of Origen's method and his own endorsement of it: 'And it was with great wisdom and sagacity that he acted on this principle'. Argument 15 adds the limit: on divine things Origen 'counselled us to attach ourselves to none of them, not even though they were attested as most wise by all men, but to devote ourselves to God alone, and to the prophets.' Not in the candidate pool, but a strong contemporary witness for Origen.

stances.summary: Young Christians should read the pagan poets, historians and philosophers, but like bees: take the honey that agrees with the truth and pass over the rest.
stances.quote: So we, if wise, shall take from heathen books whatever befits us and is allied to the truth, and shall pass over the rest. And just as in culling roses we avoid the thorns, from such writings as these we will gather everything useful, and guard against the noxious.
stances.translation: F. M. Padelford, Essays on the Study and Use of Poetry by Plutarch and Basil the Great (Yale Studies in English 15), 1902
stances.work: Address to Young Men on the Right Use of Greek Literature
stances.context: A whole treatise on the subject, the most famous patristic defence of reading the classics, written for his nephews (date disputed, usually the 360s-370s). Section 2 of the same page: 'Consequently we must be conversant with poets, with historians, with orators, indeed with all men who may further our soul's salvation.' The pagan books come first as training, 'then at length' the Scriptures. The limit is strict: stop your ears to the poets' gods and vices. A personal counterweight: in Letter 223.2 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/3202223.htm, c. 375) he says 'Much time had I spent in vanity, and had wasted nearly all my youth in the vain labour which I underwent in acquiring the wisdom made foolish by God.' Basil studied at Athens with Gregory of Nazianzus. Note: the tertullian.org page is hard-wrapped and carries page markers such as '|104'; compare with whitespace collapsed.

stances.summary: Education is the first of our goods, and that includes pagan learning. Christians who despise it are wrong; take what helps and reject the idolatry.
stances.quote: I take it as admitted by men of sense, that the first of our advantages is education; and not only this our more noble form of it, which disregards rhetorical ornaments and glory, and holds to salvation, and beauty in the objects of our contemplation: but even that external culture which many Christians ill-judgingly abhor, as treacherous and dangerous, and keeping us afar from God.
stances.translation: Charles Gordon Browne and James Edward Swallow, NPNF 2nd series vol. 7, 1894 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: Oration 43, Funeral Oration on Basil the Great
stances.context: Delivered c. 381. The same section: 'We must not then dishonour education, because some men are pleased to do so, but rather suppose such men to be boorish and uneducated'. It also shows the other side existed: 'many Christians' abhorred outside culture. When the emperor Julian barred Christians from teaching the classics (362), Gregory protested in his First Invective (Oration 4.100-107; C. W. King's 1888 translation at https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_nazianzen_2_oration4.htm): 'Words alone I cleave to' and 'How did it come into thy head, thou silliest and greediest of mortals, to deprive the Christians of words?' He also wrote Christian poetry in classical metres.

stances.summary: The classics and the Bible do not mix. A Christian, and above all one vowed to Christ, should not feed on Horace, Virgil and Cicero.
stances.quote: How can Horace go with the psalter, Virgil with the gospels, Cicero with the apostle?
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893 (New Advent edition)
stances.original: Quid facit cum Psalterio Horatius? cum Evangeliis Maro? cum Apostolo Cicero?
stances.context: EARLIER VIEW, Rome 384. Section 30 tells the famous dream: he would 'fast only that I might afterwards read Cicero', was hauled before the Judge and told 'You lie. You are a follower of Cicero and not of Christ', and swore: 'Lord, if ever again I possess worldly books, or if ever again I read such, I have denied You.' (Latin of the rebuke, checked at http://croala.ffzg.unizg.hr/eklogai/capsa/hier-epist-22/: 'Ciceronianus es, non Christianus'.) He did not keep the oath: see his later stance (Letter 70, 397) and Apology against Rufinus 1.30-31 (402, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/27101.htm): 'it was a promise for the future, not the abolition of my memory of the past' and 'a promise given in a dream must not be pressed.' Note: New Advent modernises the NPNF 'Thou liest' to 'You lie'.

stances.summary: Moses, the prophets and Paul all quoted pagan writers, and so did every great Christian author. Secular wisdom can be shaved clean of idolatry and taken as a servant of the true faith.
stances.quote: Is it surprising that I too, admiring the fairness of her form and the grace of her eloquence, desire to make that secular wisdom which is my captive and my handmaid, a matron of the true Israel?
stances.translation: W. H. Fremantle, G. Lewis and W. G. Martley, NPNF 2nd series vol. 6, 1893 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: Letter 70, to Magnus, an orator of Rome
stances.context: LATER VIEW, Bethlehem 397, thirteen years after Letter 22. Magnus had asked why Jerome quoted secular authors and so 'defile[d] the whiteness of the church'. Jerome replies with Paul quoting Epimenides, Menander and Aratus, the captive woman of Deuteronomy 21 shaved and taken as wife, and a long roll of Christian writers from Quadratus to Hilary. Section 4 calls Clement 'in my judgment the most learned of men'. Section 6: 'almost all the books of all these writers ... are extremely full of erudition and philosophy.' He suspects Rufinus is behind the question. This is a real change of mind, or at least of emphasis; both letters are his.

stances.summary: Whatever the philosophers, especially the Platonists, said that is true belongs to God. Christians should claim it and put it to better use, as Israel carried Egypt's gold out of Egypt.
stances.quote: Moreover, if those who are called philosophers, and especially the Platonists, have said anything that is true and in harmony with our faith, we are not only not to shrink from it, but to claim it for our own use from those who have unlawful possession of it.
stances.translation: James Shaw, NPNF 1st series vol. 2, 1887 (New Advent edition)
stances.original: Philosophi autem qui vocantur, si qua forte vera et fidei nostrae accomodata dixerunt, maxime Platonici, non solum formidanda non sunt, sed ab eis etiam tamquam ab iniustis possessoribus in usum nostrum vindicanda.
stances.context: Book 2 written c. 396-397. The Egyptian gold follows, and 2.40.61 names Cyprian, Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus and Hilary as Christians who carried it out. Also 2.18.28: 'let every good and true Christian understand that wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master'. Latin checked at https://www.augustinus.it/latino/dottrina_cristiana/dottrina_cristiana_2_libro.htm. His own story: Cicero's Hortensius 'changed my affections, and turned my prayers to Yourself, O Lord' (Confessions 3.4) and 'certain books of the Platonists' prepared his conversion (Confessions 7.9). Late qualification, not reversal: Retractations 1.1.4 (c. 427), my rendering of the Latin at https://www.augustinus.it/latino/ritrattazioni/ritrattazioni_1_libro.htm: 'The very praise with which I extolled Plato or the Platonists or the Academic philosophers, more than was fitting for ungodly men, has rightly displeased me, especially since Christian teaching must be defended against their great errors.'

stances.summary: Christ and the apostles neither called Greek learning inspired nor banned it. Many Greek philosophers came close to knowing God, and their training in reasoning equips Christians to answer opponents.
stances.quote: Greek literature certainly was never recognized either by Christ or his Apostles as divinely inspired, nor on the other hand was it wholly rejected as pernicious. And this they did, I conceive, not inconsiderately. For there were many philosophers among the Greeks who were not far from the knowledge of God
stances.translation: A. C. Zenos, NPNF 2nd series vol. 2, 1890 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: A lay historian at Constantinople writing c. 439-450, not in the candidate pool. Written about Julian's law of 362 forbidding Christians to be taught Greek literature. He records the opposing Christian view of his day as an objection: 'pagan philosophy teaches Polytheism, and is injurious to the promotion of true religion'. His answer continues that Scripture does not 'instruct us in the art of reasoning' and 'adversaries are most easily foiled, when we can use their own weapons against them'.

stances.summary: Philosophy is the right tool for thinking about God. Reason and faith should be joined, and the great pagan philosophers are worth translating whole.
stances.quote: examine carefully what I have said, and if possible, reconcile faith and reason.
stances.translation: H. F. Stewart and E. K. Rand, Loeb Classical Library, 1918
stances.original: diligentius intuere quae dicta sunt et fidem si poterit rationemque coniunge.
stances.work: Theological Tractates: Whether Father, Son and Holy Spirit Are Substantially Predicated of the Divinity
stances.context: Rome, early 6th century; executed c. 524-525. The page is an OCR text file: collapse whitespace, and note the stray footnote mark after 'reason.' In the preface to On the Trinity (same file) he says he will 'wrap up the ideas I draw from the deep questionings of philosophy in new and unaccustomed words'. His life plan, stated in his second commentary on Aristotle's On Interpretation, Book 2 (Latin in Meiser's 1880 edition, OCR at https://archive.org/download/commentariiinlib00boetuoft/commentariiinlib00boetuoft_djvu.txt, my rendering): to translate into Latin every work of Aristotle he could get and all the dialogues of Plato, and then to show that the two 'do not, as most think, disagree in everything, but agree in most things, and those the greatest in philosophy'. The Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison, has Lady Philosophy lead him to God with no explicit Christian reference.

stances.summary: The best philosophers taught one God, so close to Christians that you could mistake one for the other. But Christians live the wisdom the philosophers only talked about, and need not revere them.
stances.quote: I have set forth the opinions almost of all the philosophers whose more illustrious glory it is to have pointed out that there is one God, although with many names; so that any one might think either that Christians are now philosophers, or that philosophers were then already Christians.
stances.translation: Robert Ernest Wallis, ANF vol. 4, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: A Roman lawyer's dialogue, c. 200-240, not in the candidate pool. The other half of the view, chapter 38: 'let Socrates the Athenian buffoon see to it ... We despise the bent brows of the philosophers, whom we know to be corrupters, and adulterers, and tyrants ... we do not speak great things, but we live them'. So: philosophers as witnesses to one God, not as teachers to follow.

stances.summary: Poets and philosophers, moved by something from God, groped toward the truth about God and got part of it, but could not grasp it fully because they learned from themselves and not from God.
stances.quote: For poets and philosophers, as to other subjects so also to this, have applied themselves in the way of conjecture, moved, by reason of their affinity with the afflatus from God, each one by his own soul, to try whether he could find out and apprehend the truth; but they have not been found competent fully to apprehend it
stances.translation: B. P. Pratten, ANF vol. 2, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Athens, c. 177, not in the candidate pool. He argues from the philosophers' own monotheism (chapters 5-7) but ranks the Spirit-led prophets above them. A classic 'partial truth' position.

stances.summary: Philosophy as a method never reached wisdom, and its schools should be abandoned for God's teaching. Yet every sect saw some piece of the truth, and whoever gathered the pieces would agree with Christians.
stances.quote: For we do not overthrow philosophy, as the Academics are accustomed to do, whose plan was to reply to everything, which is rather to calumniate and mock; but we show that no sect was so much out of the way, and no philosopher so vain, as not to see something of the truth.
stances.translation: William Fletcher, ANF vol. 7, 1886 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 303-311 by a former professor of rhetoric, 'the Christian Cicero'. The same chapter: 'But if there had been any one to collect together the truth which was dispersed among individuals and scattered among sects, and to reduce it to a body, he assuredly would not disagree with us. But no one is able to do this, unless he has experience and knowledge of the truth.' The other half: Book 3 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/07013.htm) is a whole book against philosophy; 3.2 argues 'that philosophy is not wisdom', and 3.30 ends 'Let them therefore all depart, who do not instruct human life, but throw it into confusion.' In 5.1 he complains that Cyprian failed with pagans because his writings were 'mystical' and could be heard 'by the faithful only', implying apologists must argue from reason and pagan authors.

stances.summary: Outside learning is like Pharaoh's barren daughter who adopted Moses. A beginner may keep her as a foster mother, but a mature soul should be ashamed to be called her son, because philosophy never gives birth to life.
stances.quote: For outside learning is truly barren: always in labour, never bringing a living child to birth. For what fruit has philosophy shown for all its long labour pains?
stances.translation: own rendering of the Greek of Life of Moses 2.11 as quoted verbatim by Gregory Palamas; the only full English is Malherbe and Ferguson (1978), copyrighted
stances.original: ἄγονος γάρ ὡς ἀληθῶς ἡ ἔξωθεν παίδευσις, ἀεί ὠδίνουσα καί μηδέποτε ζωογονοῦσα τῷ τοκετῷ. Τίνα γάρ ἔδειξε καρπόν τῶν μακρῶν ὠδίνων ἡ φιλοσοφία;
stances.context: Late work, c. 390. I could not load an edition of the Life of Moses itself; the Greek was read inside Gregory Palamas's Triads (section 16 on that page), which quotes it as 'what was said about Moses by [Basil's] brother'. Hence status secondary-only. The same quoted passage carries the middle view: the text 'allows one not to reject the kinship of the falsely named mother so long as one sees the immaturity of youth in oneself' (my rendering). Reported but not checked here: in 2.37-41 of the same work he reads the Egyptian spoils as outside learning that may be carried off to adorn the Church. His letters show affection for classical rhetoric (Letter 11, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/291111.htm, urges Libanius not to 'condemn oratory altogether'), while Letter 10 insists 'our teachers ... are Paul and John, and the rest of the Apostles and Prophets'.

stances.summary: A Christian should not read the poets' fictions, which stir up desire. Grammar and secular learning can still help a life if they are put to better use.
stances.quote: A Christian is forbidden to read the fictions of the poets for this reason: by the delights of empty fables they stir the mind to the kindlings of lust.
stances.translation: own rendering of the Latin
stances.original: Ideo prohibetur christianus figmenta legere poetarum quia per oblectamenta inanium fabularum mentem excitant ad incentiua libidinum.
stances.location: Book 3, chapter 13 ('On the books of the gentiles'), section 1
stances.context: Bishop of Seville, died 636; not in the candidate pool. Section 2: 'such books are to be avoided, and shunned for love of the holy Scriptures' ('Cauendi sunt igitur tales libri, et propter amorem sanctarum scripturarum uitandi'). Section 11, the concession: 'grammarians are better than heretics ... the teaching of the grammarians can even profit for life, when it is taken up for better uses' ('grammaticorum autem doctrina potest etiam proficere ad uitam, dum fuerit in meliores usus adsumpta'). His own Etymologies is an encyclopedia built largely from pagan authors.

stances.summary: Philosophy is where heresies come from. Once you have Christ and the gospel, you need no more searching; Christians should not build a faith mixed with Stoic and Platonic ideas.
stances.quote: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? What between heretics and Christians? Our instruction comes from the porch of Solomon, who had himself taught that the Lord should be sought in simplicity of heart.
stances.translation: Peter Holmes, ANF vol. 3, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.original: Quid ergo Athenis et Hierosolymis? quid academiae et ecclesiae? quid haereticis et christianis? Nostra institutio de porticu Solomonis est qui et ipse tradiderat Dominum in simplicitate cordis esse quaerendum.
stances.context: Carthage, c. 200, before his Montanist period (from c. 207). The chapter opens 'Indeed heresies are themselves instigated by philosophy' and continues 'Away with all attempts to produce a mottled Christianity of Stoic, Platonic, and dialectic composition! We want no curious disputation after possessing Christ Jesus'. Latin checked at https://www.thelatinlibrary.com/tertullian/tertullian.praescrip.shtml. His own qualifications: On Idolatry 10 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0302.htm) says 'Learning literature is allowable for believers, rather than teaching' because 'literature is the means of training for all life'; On the Soul 2 (Montanist period, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0310.htm) grants 'we shall not deny that philosophers have sometimes thought the same things as ourselves', as a ship finds harbour 'by some happy chance'; On the Soul 20 cites 'Seneca ... whom we so often find on our side', while On the Soul 3 calls philosophers 'those patriarchs of heretics'. Apology 46 asks 'where is there any likeness between the Christian and the philosopher?' He was himself steeped in Stoicism and rhetoric.

stances.summary: Greek philosophy is borrowed, quarrelsome and empty. Christians have left it behind to follow the word of God, which is older and truer.
stances.quote: Finding you to be such men as these, we have abandoned you, and no longer concern ourselves with your tenets, but follow the word of God.
stances.translation: J. E. Ryland, ANF vol. 2, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 165-175 by Justin's pupil; not in the candidate pool. A whole work against Greek learning. Chapter 29 on his conversion: 'I discern that the former class of writings lead to condemnation'. Heterodox: after Justin's death he joined or founded the Encratites (rejecting marriage and wine) and was treated as a heretic by Irenaeus. Useful as the sharpest early voice on the 'no' side, and a neat foil to his own teacher Justin.

stances.summary: The poets and philosophers gained nothing by their learning and did not know the truth. Their opinions are useless next to the prophets.
stances.quote: What did Plato's system of culture profit him? Or what benefit did the rest of the philosophers derive from their doctrines, not to enumerate the whole of them, since they are numerous? But these things we say, for the purpose of exhibiting their useless and godless opinions.
stances.translation: Marcus Dods, ANF vol. 2, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Bishop of Antioch, c. 180; not in the candidate pool. Qualification in Book 2, chapter 38 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02042.htm): the poets and philosophers 'have clearly taught both concerning righteousness, and judgment, and punishment ... though, indeed, they said this unwillingly, for they were convinced by the truth.' So he uses them as reluctant witnesses, not teachers.

stances.summary: The heretics have nothing new: they stitched their systems together out of the philosophers and the comic poets. Better to be simple and love God than to be clever and fall away.
stances.quote: they also bring together the things which have been said by all those who were ignorant of God, and who are termed philosophers; and sewing together, as it were, a motley garment out of a heap of miserable rags, they have, by their subtle manner of expression, furnished themselves with a cloak which is really not their own.
stances.translation: Alexander Roberts and William Rambaut, ANF vol. 1, 1885 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Lyons, c. 180. His target is the Valentinian Gnostics, not Christian study as such, so the stance is in passing. Against Heresies 2.26.1 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103226.htm): 'It is therefore better and more profitable to belong to the simple and unlettered class, and by means of love to attain to nearness to God'. He never tells Christians not to read philosophy, and he knew it well. Caution: his treatment of the Egyptian spoils (4.30) is about property received from pagans, not learning; do not cite him for the 'spoils' reading of education.

stances.summary: Every heresy can be traced back to a Greek philosopher. The heretics took nothing from Scripture; their doctrines grew from the wisdom of the Greeks.
stances.quote: their doctrines have derived their origin from the wisdom of the Greeks, from the conclusions of those who have formed systems of philosophy, and from would-be mysteries, and the vagaries of astrologers
stances.translation: J. H. MacMahon, ANF vol. 5, 1886 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Rome, c. 222-235. Authorship of the Refutation by Hippolytus is disputed; many scholars now say only 'the author of the Refutation'. Weak on this claim: his whole method required close study of the philosophers, and the same preface calls the philosophers 'more deserving of reverence in reference to their views respecting the divinity' than the heretics. Treat as a mild 'no'.

stances.person: Apostolic Constitutions (and the Didascalia Apostolorum behind it)
stances.summary: Stay away from pagan books altogether. The Bible already has better history, wisdom, poetry and law than all of them.
stances.quote: Abstain from all the heathen books. For what have you to do with such foreign discourses, or laws, or false prophets, which subvert the faith of the unstable? For what defect do you find in the law of God, that you should have recourse to those heathenish fables?
stances.translation: James Donaldson, ANF vol. 7, 1886 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: An anonymous church order compiled in Syria c. 375-380, reworking the Didascalia Apostolorum (3rd century, Syria), which already says (R. H. Connolly's 1929 translation at https://www.earlychristianwritings.com/text/didascalia.html, chapter 2): 'But avoid all books of the heathen.' It goes on: 'if wise men and philosophers, thou hast the Prophets'. Not a person: if the quiz needs a named figure, leave this out of results and use it only as evidence that the rule existed in church law. Connolly's 1929 English is public domain in the US only since 2025, so the ANF text is quoted here.

stances.summary: Faith needs no Greek arguments. An unlettered Christian who trusts God knows more than philosophers, and a sound mind has no need of books.
stances.quote: We Christians therefore hold the mystery not in the wisdom of Greek arguments, but in the power of faith richly supplied to us by God through Jesus Christ. And to show that this statement is true, behold now, without having learned letters, we believe in God, knowing through His works His providence over all things.
stances.translation: H. Ellershaw, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 357-362 by Athanasius, who knew Antony; the speeches are Athanasius's rendering of what Antony said through an interpreter. Chapter 73: 'Which is first, mind or letters? ... Whoever, therefore, has a sound mind has not need of letters.' Evagrius, quoted by Socrates Scholasticus (Church History 4.23, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/26014.htm), gives Antony's answer to a philosopher: 'My book, O philosopher ... is the nature of things that are made, and it is present whenever I wish to read the words of God.' He does not forbid learning; he finds it unnecessary.

stances.summary: The Greek philosophers wrote a great deal with skill, but achieved nothing next to the Cross. Since Christ came, their wisdom is fading away.
stances.quote: The philosophers of the Greeks have composed many works with plausibility and verbal skill; what result, then, have they exhibited so great as has the Cross of Christ?
stances.translation: Archibald Robertson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 4, 1892 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 318-337. Chapter 55: 'not only does the wisdom of the Greeks no longer advance, but what there is is now fading away'. Weak evidence on the claim as worded: this is an apologetic boast about the Cross, not a rule against study, and Athanasius himself argues in philosophical terms in Against the Heathen. Use only as a mild 'no', or leave out.

stances.summary: Probing God with clever argument is a Greek disease. Faith rests on Abraham and the prophets, not on Greek disputation.
stances.quote: Accursed disputation, that hidden moth, is from the Greeks.
stances.translation: J. B. Morris (1847), reprinted in NPNF 2nd series vol. 13, 1898 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: The Pearl: Seven Hymns on the Faith (Hymns on Faith 81-87)
stances.context: Nisibis and Edessa, c. 360s. Aimed at the 'disputers' of the Arian controversy who tried to 'explore' the Son and the Spirit 'with their questionings'. Stanza 1: 'The sound form of our faith is from Abraham'. His target is Greek-style speculation about God rather than all reading. A sharper line often quoted as his ('Blessed is he who has not tasted the poison of the wisdom of the Greeks', said to be Hymns on Faith 2.24) could not be checked in any public-domain text; see notes.

stances.summary: Having searched the philosophers and found them wanting, the soul must hold to the Apostle's warning and not linger in pagan philosophy.
stances.quote: And lest the soul should stray and linger in some delusion of heathen philosophy, it receives this further lesson of perfect loyalty to the holy faith, taught by the Apostle in words inspired:— Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the word, and not after Christ
stances.translation: E. W. Watson and L. Pullan, NPNF 2nd series vol. 9, 1899 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written c. 356-360. Book 1 opens with his own search: he began with the philosophers' ideas of the good life and found rest only in Scripture. Section 18 warns the reader 'to eschew the feeble and baseless conjectures of earthly minds'. Jerome (Letter 70.5) says Hilary imitated Quintilian in style, so he did not renounce classical rhetoric. Mild 'no'.

stances.summary: Pagan philosophers could say whatever they liked about the soul. Christians may not: Scripture is the rule and measure of every teaching, so set Plato aside.
stances.quote: we are not entitled to such licence, I mean that of affirming what we please; we make the Holy Scriptures the rule and the measure of every tenet; we necessarily fix our eyes upon that, and approve that alone which may be made to harmonize with the intention of those writings.
stances.translation: William Moore and Henry Austin Wilson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 5, 1893 (New Advent edition)
stances.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection, by Gregory of Nyssa
stances.location: the section on desire and anger (Macrina speaking)
stances.context: A dialogue written by her brother Gregory c. 380-383 after her death in 379, so her words are his literary record. Next sentence: 'We must therefore neglect the Platonic chariot and the pair of horses'. Qualification: in the same dialogue she says thinkers 'outside our own system of thought' have 'approached and touched the doctrine of the Resurrection', and the whole dialogue argues philosophically. Gregory's Life of Macrina (W. K. Lowther Clarke's 1916 translation, https://www.tertullian.org/fathers/gregory_macrina_1_life.htm) says she drew Basil, 'puffed up beyond measure with the pride of oratory', toward the ascetic life, and raised her brother Peter 'in holy studies, so as not to give his soul leisure to turn to vain things'. Her mother had her taught Scripture instead of the poets.

stances.summary: God did not choose to save His people by logic. Faith is simple; the heretics hide their poison in dialectic, and whatever is good in the philosophers came from Scripture first.
stances.quote: For they store up all the strength of their poisons in dialetical disputation, which by the judgment of philosophers is defined as having no power to establish anything, and aiming only at destruction. But it was not by dialectic that it pleased God to save His people; for the kingdom of God consists in simplicity of faith, not in wordy contention.
stances.translation: H. de Romestin, E. de Romestin and H. T. F. Duckworth, NPNF 2nd series vol. 10, 1896 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Milan, 378. 'dialetical' is the page's spelling. Book 1.13.84: 'Away with arguments, where faith is required; now let dialectic hold her peace ... Not philosophers but fishermen ... now find credence.' In practice he was deeply read: his Duties of the Clergy is modelled on Cicero's De officiis (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34011.htm, 1.24), and there he claims 'Pythagoras himself, who lived before the time of Socrates, followed the prophet David's steps and gave his disciples a law of silence' (1.31), i.e. whatever is right in the philosophers was taken from Scripture. So his stated view is 'no', his practice is heavy use.

stances.summary: Plato spent his life on useless cobwebs and persuaded no one, while unlearned fishermen won the world. Greek philosophy is worthless next to the Christian life.
stances.quote: What great labors did Plato endure, and his followers, discoursing to us about a line, and an angle, and a point, and about numbers even and odd, and equal unto one another and unequal, and such-like spiderwebs; (for indeed those webs are not more useless to man's life than were these subjects;)
stances.translation: Talbot W. Chambers, NPNF 1st series vol. 12, 1889 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Antioch, c. 390s; he was himself trained by the pagan rhetor Libanius. Repeated across his preaching: Homily 4 also says God 'cast out Plato for example, not by means of another philosopher of more skill, but by an unlearned fisherman'; Homily 1 on Matthew (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/200101.htm) mocks 'Plato, who composed that ridiculous Republic'; Homily 21 on Ephesians (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230121.htm) calls it 'that worthless philosophy of theirs, (for such the Grecian philosophy is,)' and blames 'the heathen tales' of Achilles for corrupting boys, while taking ordinary schooling for granted. Homily 3 on First Corinthians (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/220103.htm) is careful not to reject learned converts 'on account of their Gentile wisdom'. For him 'philosophy' properly means the Christian, especially monastic, way of life.

stances.summary: A heart given to Christ refuses the Muses. The cunning of the philosophers, the art of the rhetoricians and the fictions of the poets cloud the light of God; they cannot hold what is good or true without God.
stances.quote: Hearts vowed to Christ say no to the Muses and are shut to Apollo.
stances.translation: own rendering of the Latin
stances.original: Negant Camoenis, nec patent Apollini Dicata Christo pectora.
stances.location: the iambic section, answering his old teacher's plea that he return to poetry
stances.context: Written c. 389-393 after his conversion, to his former teacher, the poet Ausonius, who begged him to come back to the Muses. The lines before: 'Quid abdicatas in meam curam, pater, / Redire Musas praecipis?' ('Why, father, do you bid the Muses I renounced return to my care?'). A few lines on (same page, my rendering): God 'forbids us to give our leisure or our business to empty things and to the literature of fables, so that we may obey His laws and see His light, which the cunning force of the philosophers, the art of the rhetoricians and the fictions of the poets cloud over' ('Vacare vanis otio aut negotio, / Et fabulosis litteris / Vetat ... Quam vis sophorum callida, arsque rhetorum, et / Figmenta vatum nubilant'), and 'what good or true can they hold who do not hold the Head of all, God?' Qualification: he went on writing fine Christian poetry in classical metres (the poems for St Felix), so he rejected pagan content and inspiration, not form.

stances.summary: Worldly learning does not make a soul wise before God. The highly educated Arsenius said an Egyptian peasant knew an alphabet of the spirit he had never learned.
stances.quote: With Greek and Latin learning I am well acquainted, but I have not yet learned the alphabet of this villager.
stances.translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Paradise or Garden of the Holy Fathers, vol. 2, 1907 (from the Syriac of Anan-Isho)
stances.work: Sayings of the Desert Fathers (Budge's Paradise, Questions and Answers on the Ascetic Rule)
stances.location: saying 234 (Budge's numbering), p. 202; corresponds to Arsenius 6 in the Greek alphabetical collection
stances.context: Arsenius (c. 350-445) had been a learned tutor at the imperial court before fleeing to the Egyptian desert. The page is raw OCR: each continued line starts with a stray quotation mark, so strip those and collapse whitespace before comparing. Saying 233 just above: asked why unlearned Egyptian villagers have such virtues, 'Abba Arsenius (or Abba Macarius)' answers: 'We possess nothing whatsoever of the learning of the world, but these Egyptian villagers have acquired spiritual excellences through their labours.' (the OCR breaks 'pos-sess' across two lines). This is about spiritual progress, not a ban on study. The common modern English wording (Benedicta Ward, 1975) is copyrighted; do not use it.

stances.summary: A literary education clogs the mind: the poets' stories and battle scenes come back even in prayer. The cure is to pour the same zeal into Scripture until it drives them out.
stances.quote: a special hindrance to salvation is added by that knowledge of literature which I seem already to have in some slight measure attained, in which the efforts of my tutor, or my attention to continual reading have so weakened me that now my mind is filled with those songs of the poets so that even at the hour of prayer it is thinking about those trifling fables
stances.translation: C. S. Gibson, NPNF 2nd series vol. 11, 1894 (New Advent edition)
stances.context: Written in Gaul c. 426-429, about his time in Egypt. Unusually, Cassian speaks here in the first person. Nesteros answers (chapter 13): 'transfer to the reading of and meditation upon the writings of the Spirit, the same diligence and earnestness which you say that you showed in those secular studies of yours'. The objection is to the classics as a distraction in prayer, not a doctrinal ban.

stances.summary: Benedict left his studies in Rome because he saw learning lead young men into loose living. He chose to serve God alone, wisely unlearned.
stances.quote: wherefore, giving over his book, and forsaking his father's house and wealth, with a resolute mind only to serve God, he sought for some place, where he might attain to the desire of his holy purpose: and in this sort he departed, instructed with learned ignorance, and furnished with unlearned wisdom.
stances.translation: P. W. (1608), revised by Edmund G. Gardner, The Dialogues of Saint Gregory, 1911
stances.work: Dialogues, Book 2 (Life of Benedict), by Gregory the Great
stances.context: Written c. 593-594, about fifty years after Benedict's death, from the accounts of four of his disciples whom Gregory names. These are Gregory's words about Benedict's choice, not Benedict's own. The sentence before: 'for as much as he saw many by reason of such learning to fall to dissolute and lewd life, he drew back his foot'. Benedict's own Rule (ch. 73) recommends only Scripture and the Fathers (Cassian, Basil) for reading and never mentions pagan books; that is an argument from silence. The page is hard-wrapped with double spaces; compare with whitespace collapsed.

stances.summary: A bishop must not teach the pagan classics. The praises of Christ and the praises of Jupiter cannot share one mouth.
stances.quote: This thing we took so much amiss, and so strongly disapproved it, that we changed what had been said before into groaning and sadness, since the praises of Christ cannot find room in one mouth with the praises of Jupiter.
stances.translation: James Barmby, NPNF 2nd series vol. 13, 1898 (New Advent edition)
stances.location: Book 11, Letter 54, to Desiderius, bishop of Vienne (Book 11, Letter 34 in the modern numbering)
stances.context: Rome, 601. Desiderius was 'expounding grammar', that is, teaching the pagan poets. The letter ends hoping 'that you do not apply yourself to trifles and secular literature'. Scholars debate whether Gregory objects to all classical study or to a bishop teaching it; Gregory was himself well educated. He also praises Benedict as 'instructed with learned ignorance' (see Benedict). A later legend that he burned pagan libraries is unfounded (see misattributions).

splits_fathers: Real voices on both sides, and contemporaries say so. Clement (c. 200) reports that some thought Greek philosophy 'set a-going by the devil'; Gregory of Nazianzus (c. 381) says 'many Christians ill-judgingly abhor' pagan culture; Socrates Scholasticus (c. 440) answers Christians who said pagan philosophy 'teaches Polytheism'. The learned mainstream took the qualified 'yes', and by the late fourth century it had become the settled view of the great bishops: Justin, Clement, Origen, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Augustine, the later Jerome, Boethius (use it selectively, like bees or like Israel taking Egypt's gold, with Scripture as judge). The 'no' side has three strands: polemical rejection of philosophy as the root of heresy (Tatian, Tertullian, Irenaeus, the Refutation), church-order rules and pastoral rebukes against pagan books (Didascalia and Apostolic Constitutions, Chrysostom, the young Jerome, Paulinus, Gregory the Great), and the desert view that learning is simply unneeded or a distraction in prayer (Antony, Arsenius, Cassian, Benedict). Almost no one held either extreme purely: Tertullian let believers learn literature and cited Seneca as 'on our side'; Clement and Basil kept Scripture above all; Jerome swore off the classics in 384 and defended them in 397. The best strength-2 matches for a result: Justin, Clement, Origen, Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Augustine, Jerome (397) and Boethius on 'yes'; Tertullian, Tatian, Jerome (384), Chrysostom, Paulinus and Gregory the Great on 'no'.
splits_people_today: As worded, most people today would agree: secular people take it for granted, and most Catholics, Orthodox, mainline Protestants and the classical-education and C. S. Lewis wing of evangelicals agree strongly. A real minority disagrees: some fundamentalist, separatist and 'Bible only' homeschool circles, some Reformed thinkers wary of 'secular philosophy' (reading Colossians 2:8 as Tertullian did), and some charismatic and pietist Christians who say you need only the Bible and the Spirit. A few secular people also disagree from the other direction, holding that faith and philosophy cannot mix. So the claim is lopsided today, though not unanimous. To make it split, frame the 'no' so it sounds reasonable, for example 'Time spent on philosophy would be better spent on the Bible' or 'I don't need non-Christian thinkers to understand life'. Among the Fathers the split is real, with a learned majority for the qualified 'yes'.

misattributions.line: Credo quia absurdum (I believe because it is absurd)
misattributions.truth: Not in his works. The nearest is On the Flesh of Christ 5, about the death of the Son of God: 'it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd' (Latin 'prorsus credibile est, quia ineptum est'), https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0315.htm. It is a paradox about the Cross, not a general attack on reason, and the famous Latin slogan is a later coinage.

Not his words. It paraphrases On Christian Doctrine 2.18.28: 'wherever truth may be found, it belongs to his Master' (Latin 'Domini sui esse intellegat, ubicumque invenerit veritatem'). The slogan was popularised by Arthur F. Holmes's book 'All Truth Is God's Truth' (1977). Quote the real sentence instead.

misattributions.line: What is Plato but Moses speaking Attic Greek?
misattributions.truth: Clement quotes it (Stromata 1.22, https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/02101.htm) from Numenius, a pagan Pythagorean philosopher: 'And Numenius, the Pythagorean philosopher, expressly writes: For what is Plato, but Moses speaking in Attic Greek?' Not a Christian's own line.

misattributions.line: Pope Gregory the Great burned the Palatine library (or the books of Livy) to stop people reading the classics
misattributions.truth: A later medieval story, usually traced to John of Salisbury in the 12th century. Nothing from Gregory's own time supports it. I did not check the medieval text itself. His real, verifiable rebuke is the letter to Desiderius.

misattributions.line: Irenaeus first read 'spoiling the Egyptians' as permission to use pagan learning
misattributions.truth: Against Heresies 4.30 (https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/0103430.htm) uses the Egyptian spoils to defend Christians' use of property received from pagans, not learning. The learning reading begins with Origen's Letter to Gregory and is made famous by Augustine.

notes: 1. Quoting and checking. New Advent pages reproduce the ANF and NPNF translations but lightly modernise them (for example 'You lie' for the NPNF 'Thou liest', 'you' for 'thou'); every quotation above is copied from New Advent, so check against New Advent, not CCEL. The tertullian.org pages (Basil, Gregory's Dialogues) are hard-wrapped with double spaces and page markers, and the archive.org texts (Budge, Boethius) are raw OCR with stray quotation marks at line starts and footnote marks: normalise whitespace and strip those marks before a substring check. For the three own renderings (Gregory of Nyssa, Isidore, Paulinus) check the 'original' field against the url, not the English. 2. The reader-facing question is fairer if it separates two things the Fathers separated: reading pagan literature for skill and style (widely allowed, even by Tertullian) and taking truth about God and life from pagan thinkers (the real dispute). The sharpest pairs for a reveal: Justin versus his own pupil Tatian; Tertullian ('What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem?') versus Clement (philosophy 'a schoolmaster to bring the Hellenic mind ... to Christ'), both writing c. 200; Jerome against Jerome (384 versus 397); Basil's bees versus Chrysostom's 'spiderwebs'; Augustine's Egyptian gold versus Gregory the Great's 'praises of Jupiter'. 3. Unverified and not used: 'Blessed is he who has not tasted the poison of the wisdom of the Greeks', said to be Ephrem, Hymns on Faith 2.24; I found no public-domain English and could not check the Syriac, so do not publish it without checking Beck's edition. Gregory of Nyssa's Life of Moses 2.37-41 (Egyptian spoils as learning for the Church) is widely cited but I could not load the Greek; only 2.10-12 was read, via Palamas. Cassiodorus (Institutions, c. 550, a strong 'yes' for secular learning in monasteries) is a good lead, but I could not load a text. 4. Common misreadings: Tertullian's Athens line is often taken as a rejection of all learning, but the same author allowed Christians to learn literature (On Idolatry 10); and Jerome's dream is often told as if he gave up the classics for good, which he did not (Letter 70; Apology against Rufinus 1.30-31). 5. Nothing clear was found for Ignatius, Perpetua, Cyprian, Novatian, Martin of Tours, Syncletica, Moses the Black, Poemen, Evagrius, Pelagius, John Climacus or Isaac the Syrian on this question. Cyprian's own writings avoid pagan authors, but that is a scholarly observation, not a statement of his; Augustine (On Christian Doctrine 2.40.61) and Jerome (Letter 70) count him among those who carried out Egypt's gold. Evagrius appears only as the source of Antony's 'my book is the nature of created things'. 6. Heterodox or disputed figures in this file: Origen (posthumously condemned in part), Tatian (Encratite), Tertullian (Montanist after c. 207; his key text here predates that), and the Refutation (authorship disputed).
